questionText: What is the Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)?
option1: A class should never be extended
option2: A class should have only one public method
option3: A class should implement only one interface
option4: A class should have only one reason to change
correctOptionExplanation: SRP states a class should have exactly one reason to change, meaning it should be responsible for one cohesive piece of functionality.

questionText: Which SOLID letter does SRP represent?
option1: D
option2: L
option3: S
option4: O
correctOptionExplanation: SRP is the 'S' in SOLID.

questionText: A class named DBManager has two methods: one that writes/constructs SQL queries and one that runs them against the database. Why does this violate SRP?
option1: It has too many public fields
option2: It uses inheritance incorrectly
option3: It doesn't implement an interface
option4: It has two separate reasons to change: query-construction logic and query-execution/connection logic
correctOptionExplanation: Query syntax changing and database execution/connection mechanics changing are two independent reasons to modify the class, which is exactly what SRP warns against combining.

questionText: What is the SRP-compliant fix for the DBManager example above?
option1: Add more methods to DBManager to handle every case
option2: Make all methods in DBManager private
option3: Split it into DBQueryManager (builds queries) and DBQueryRunner (executes queries)
option4: Merge DBManager with the class that calls it
correctOptionExplanation: Separating query construction from query execution gives each resulting class exactly one reason to change.

questionText: After splitting into DBQueryManager and DBQueryRunner, if the SQL dialect/query syntax changes, which class should you modify?
option1: Only DBQueryRunner
option2: Both classes equally
option3: Neither, since SRP prevents any changes
option4: Only DBQueryManager
correctOptionExplanation: DBQueryManager owns query construction, so syntax changes are isolated there; DBQueryRunner (execution) remains untouched.

questionText: If instead the JDBC driver/connection execution mechanism changes, which class should you modify?
option1: Only DBQueryManager
option2: Neither class, modify the calling code instead
option3: Both classes equally
option4: Only DBQueryRunner
correctOptionExplanation: DBQueryRunner owns execution details, so connection/driver changes are isolated there without touching query-building logic.

questionText: What is the main benefit of this DBQueryManager/DBQueryRunner separation for testing?
option1: Tests automatically run faster with no code changes
option2: You no longer need to write any tests
option3: You can unit test query construction without needing a real database connection
option4: It removes the need for a database entirely
correctOptionExplanation: Because query building is isolated in DBQueryManager, its logic can be tested without spinning up an actual database dependency.

questionText: Does SRP mean a class must contain only a single method?
option1: Yes, exactly one method per class always
option2: No, SRP has nothing to do with methods at all
option3: No, it means one reason to change; a class can have multiple methods if they all serve one cohesive responsibility
option4: Yes, but only for abstract classes
correctOptionExplanation: SRP is about a single reason to change, not raw method count — several tightly related methods serving one purpose is still SRP-compliant.

questionText: A Report class both calculates report data and formats/prints it to PDF. What SRP violation does this show?
option1: Two responsibilities (calculation logic and presentation/formatting logic) bundled into one class
option2: A Liskov Substitution violation
option3: No violation, since both relate to 'reports'
option4: An Open/Closed violation only
correctOptionExplanation: Calculating data and formatting/printing it are different reasons to change (business logic vs. presentation), so bundling them violates SRP.

questionText: What's the SRP-compliant fix for the Report example?
option1: Make the calculate method private
option2: Merge the class into the main() method
option3: Split into ReportCalculator and ReportPrinter (or ReportFormatter)
option4: Add a boolean flag to switch between calculating and printing
correctOptionExplanation: Separating calculation from presentation isolates each responsibility into its own class, each with a single reason to change.

questionText: How does SRP relate to the concept of 'cohesion' in a class?
option1: Cohesion and SRP are unrelated concepts
option2: SRP decreases cohesion by adding more methods
option3: SRP only concerns coupling, never cohesion
option4: SRP increases cohesion — a class's methods and fields all serve one focused purpose
correctOptionExplanation: A class following SRP tends to be highly cohesive: everything inside it exists to serve its single responsibility.

questionText: How does SRP relate to the concept of 'coupling' between classes?
option1: SRP has no relationship with coupling
option2: SRP eliminates coupling entirely, everywhere
option3: SRP always increases coupling between classes
option4: SRP reduces coupling, since unrelated concerns live in separate classes instead of being tangled together
correctOptionExplanation: By separating unrelated responsibilities, SRP naturally reduces the ways in which unrelated logic depends on or affects each other.

questionText: What real-world team benefit does SRP provide on a growing codebase?
option1: It guarantees zero bugs in the codebase
option2: It forces exactly one developer to ever touch the codebase
option3: Different developers or teams can own and modify separate, focused classes with less risk of stepping on each other's changes
option4: It eliminates the need for version control
correctOptionExplanation: Smaller, focused classes reduce merge conflicts and let teams work on different responsibilities (e.g., DB layer vs. business logic) independently.

questionText: What is a 'God class' (or God object) and how does it relate to SRP?
option1: A synonym for an abstract class
option2: A class that only contains static methods
option3: A class that can never be instantiated
option4: A class that has taken on far too many unrelated responsibilities, the classic anti-pattern SRP is meant to prevent
correctOptionExplanation: A God class accumulates many unrelated responsibilities over time, becoming hard to understand, test, and safely modify — exactly what SRP guards against.

questionText: Which of these is a common 'smell' suggesting an SRP violation?
option1: A class name and method list that keep growing to include unrelated behaviors over time
option2: A class with a single, well-named public method
option3: A class with private fields and public getters
option4: A class that implements one small interface
correctOptionExplanation: Classes that keep absorbing unrelated behavior (and often get vague names like 'Manager' or 'Helper') are a classic sign of accumulating multiple responsibilities.

questionText: An Employee class calculates salary, generates a PDF payslip, and saves records to the database. How many reasons to change does this class have?
option1: Two, because PDF generation and saving are the same concern
option2: Three separate reasons: salary rules, payslip formatting, and persistence/storage logic
option3: Zero, since methods don't count as reasons to change
option4: One, since it's all about the employee
correctOptionExplanation: Salary calculation, PDF formatting, and database persistence are three independent concerns that can each change for unrelated reasons.

questionText: What's the SRP-compliant refactor for the Employee example?
option1: Rename the class to EmployeeManager
option2: Combine it with a Department class
option3: Turn all methods into static utility methods
option4: Split into SalaryCalculator, PayslipGenerator, and EmployeeRepository classes
correctOptionExplanation: Each extracted class now has a single, focused responsibility and its own independent reason to change.

questionText: After the Employee refactor, if the PDF payslip layout needs to change, which class is affected?
option1: Only SalaryCalculator
option2: All three classes must change
option3: Only PayslipGenerator
option4: Only EmployeeRepository
correctOptionExplanation: Layout/formatting concerns are isolated to PayslipGenerator, so salary logic and persistence remain untouched.

questionText: What refactoring technique is commonly used to fix an SRP violation?
option1: Rename Variable
option2: Inline Method
option3: Extract Constant
option4: Extract Class — pulling unrelated behavior out into a new, focused class
correctOptionExplanation: Extract Class is the standard refactoring for splitting a class with multiple responsibilities into several single-responsibility classes.

questionText: Under Robert C. Martin's refined definition, what does 'a reason to change' really correspond to?
option1: A distinct actor/stakeholder who could request that specific kind of change
option2: The number of public methods in the class
option3: The number of lines of code in the class
option4: The number of fields in the class
correctOptionExplanation: Uncle Bob's later clarification ties 'reason to change' to distinct actors/stakeholders — each responsibility should map to one stakeholder who could request changes to it.

questionText: Using the actor-based definition, does an Employee class handling salary rules (HR's concern) and tax reporting (Finance's concern) violate SRP even if merged into 'employee logic'?
option1: Yes, because HR and Finance are different actors who could independently request changes
option2: No, since tax reporting is not really a responsibility
option3: Only if the class also handles UI rendering
option4: No, because it's all about one employee entity
correctOptionExplanation: Different stakeholders (actors) needing independent changes to the same class is the core signal of an SRP violation, even if the domain 'feels' related.

questionText: Does having multiple methods in a class automatically violate SRP?
option1: No, only if those methods serve unrelated responsibilities or different actors
option2: Yes, but only in abstract classes
option3: No, SRP only cares about field count
option4: Yes, always, no matter what the methods do
correctOptionExplanation: Multiple methods are fine as long as they all support one cohesive responsibility; the violation is about unrelated concerns, not method count.

questionText: How does SRP make debugging easier?
option1: It automatically prevents all bugs from occurring
option2: It guarantees the bug is always in the constructor
option3: It removes the need for a debugger
option4: A bug in one responsibility is isolated to a smaller, focused class instead of being tangled with unrelated logic
correctOptionExplanation: Because SRP-compliant classes bundle only related logic, tracing a bug to its source is faster since the search space per class is smaller and more focused.

questionText: What's the relationship between SRP and the Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)?
option1: ISP is about classes; SRP is about interfaces
option2: There is no meaningful relationship at all
option3: Both aim for focus and cohesion — SRP applies to classes having one reason to change, ISP applies to interfaces having small, focused contracts
option4: They are the exact same principle applied twice
correctOptionExplanation: SRP and ISP are closely related cousins in SOLID: both push toward smaller, more focused units, one for classes and one for interfaces.

questionText: From the course notes, what is stated as the overall aim behind applying SOLID principles like SRP?
option1: To make all classes abstract
option2: To keep code readable and maintainable so people need to touch as little of the codebase as possible when making changes
option3: To maximize the number of classes in a project
option4: To remove the need for any documentation
correctOptionExplanation: The class notes describe the goal of SOLID as readable, maintainable code where changes require touching as little existing code as possible.

questionText: From the course notes, what's the difference between 'tightly coupled' and 'loosely coupled' (decoupled) systems?
option1: They mean the same thing, just different wording
option2: Loosely coupled code cannot use inheritance at all
option3: Tightly coupled code has parts that depend heavily on each other's internals; loosely coupled code keeps parts independent so changes don't ripple across the system
option4: Tightly coupled always refers to interfaces; loosely coupled always refers to abstract classes
correctOptionExplanation: Tight coupling means changes in one part force changes elsewhere; loose coupling (decoupling) isolates parts so they can change independently — a direct byproduct of good SRP design.

questionText: Why does violating SRP tend to increase regression risk when making a change?
option1: Regression risk is unrelated to SRP
option2: Because SRP violations always cause compile errors
option3: Because classes with one responsibility always have more bugs
option4: Because unrelated behaviors are bundled together, a change meant for one responsibility can accidentally break another, unrelated one in the same class
correctOptionExplanation: When multiple unrelated responsibilities share a class, editing code for one concern risks unintentionally affecting the other, increasing the chance of regressions.

questionText: Which of these three method groups combined in a single class would most clearly violate SRP: parsing a file, validating the parsed data, and sending an email notification?
option1: No, since all three relate to 'processing' one file
option2: Only if the class also has a main method
option3: Yes — these are three distinct responsibilities (I/O parsing, business validation, notification) with different reasons to change
option4: No, because email sending is just a side effect, not a responsibility
correctOptionExplanation: Parsing, validation, and notification are independently changeable concerns typically owned by different parts of a system, making this a textbook SRP violation.

questionText: What's a key practical benefit of SRP for onboarding new developers to a codebase?
option1: It guarantees new developers write zero bugs
option2: New developers never need to read any code
option3: Smaller, focused classes are easier and faster to understand than large classes handling many unrelated things
option4: It removes the need for code reviews
correctOptionExplanation: Focused, single-purpose classes are quicker to learn and reason about than sprawling classes juggling many responsibilities.

questionText: How does SRP typically reduce merge conflicts in a team using version control?
option1: Because different responsibilities live in separate classes/files, developers working on different concerns rarely touch the same lines of code
option2: It automatically resolves all merge conflicts for you
option3: It prevents more than one developer from ever touching the repository
option4: Merge conflicts are unrelated to class design
correctOptionExplanation: Splitting responsibilities into separate classes/files means concurrent work on different concerns is far less likely to collide in the same file.

questionText: Does SRP inherently require the use of interfaces to be followed correctly?
option1: Yes, but only abstract classes count
option2: No, SRP is about separating responsibilities into focused classes; interfaces aren't required, though they can help elsewhere (like OCP/DIP)
option3: No, SRP can only be applied to static classes
option4: Yes, every SRP-compliant class must implement an interface
correctOptionExplanation: SRP is satisfied by splitting responsibilities into separate, focused classes — plain classes without interfaces can still be fully SRP-compliant.

questionText: What common misconception about SRP is important to avoid?
option1: That SRP simply means 'make classes small' rather than 'give each class one reason to change'
option2: That SRP was proposed by Robert C. Martin
option3: That SRP applies to classes
option4: That SRP is part of SOLID
correctOptionExplanation: Class size is a side effect, not the actual definition; SRP is fundamentally about isolating distinct reasons to change, regardless of how many lines that takes.

questionText: If a class currently has one responsibility but requirements later grow it into handling three unrelated concerns, what should you do?
option1: Refactor by extracting the newly added unrelated concerns into their own classes to restore SRP compliance
option2: Leave it as is since it already compiles and runs
option3: Rename the class to something vaguer so it 'covers' all three concerns
option4: Make all its methods private to hide the problem
correctOptionExplanation: SRP isn't a one-time check; as responsibilities creep in over time, extracting them back into focused classes keeps the design compliant.

questionText: Which of the following best distinguishes SRP from the Open/Closed Principle?
option1: They are exactly the same principle
option2: OCP only applies to database code
option3: SRP is about how many reasons a class has to change; OCP is about extending behavior without modifying existing, tested code
option4: SRP is about interfaces; OCP is about classes
correctOptionExplanation: SRP concerns responsibility separation within a class; OCP concerns how new behavior is added without editing stable existing code — related but distinct SOLID principles.

questionText: In an SRP-compliant DBQueryManager/DBQueryRunner split, what should DBQueryRunner NOT need to know about?
option1: How to execute a query against a connection
option2: How to receive an already-built query to run
option3: How to construct or build the actual SQL query strings
option4: How to return query results
correctOptionExplanation: Query construction is DBQueryManager's job; DBQueryRunner should only need a ready-made query to execute, keeping its single responsibility intact.

questionText: Why might excessive, premature splitting of classes under the banner of SRP become a problem?
option1: SRP has no possible downsides ever
option2: It always improves performance with no trade-offs
option3: It removes the need for any interfaces
option4: Over-fragmenting responsibilities that don't actually have independent reasons to change can add unnecessary complexity and indirection
correctOptionExplanation: SRP should reflect genuinely distinct reasons to change; splitting classes that don't have separate change drivers just adds needless complexity.

questionText: A UserController handles HTTP request parsing, business validation, and direct SQL queries all in one class. What's the SRP-based critique?
option1: It's fine since 'User' ties them together conceptually
option2: It bundles three distinct concerns (web layer, business rules, data access) that each have independent reasons to change
option3: It only violates encapsulation, not SRP
option4: It violates the Liskov Substitution Principle instead
correctOptionExplanation: Request parsing, business logic, and data access are classic layers that should be separated since each changes for different reasons (API contract changes, business rule changes, schema changes).

questionText: What's the SRP-friendly fix for the UserController example?
option1: Separate into a Controller (HTTP layer), a Service (business logic), and a Repository (data access)
option2: Convert all methods to static
option3: Add more parameters to the existing methods
option4: Merge it with the database configuration class
correctOptionExplanation: Layering into Controller/Service/Repository gives each layer one responsibility and one reason to change, a very common SRP-driven architecture.

questionText: How does SRP help reduce the 'blast radius' of a code change?
option1: It has no effect on the blast radius of changes
option2: Because each class has a narrow, well-defined responsibility, a change is far less likely to have unintended effects on unrelated behavior
option3: It guarantees changes never need testing
option4: It only affects private methods
correctOptionExplanation: Narrow, focused responsibilities mean edits stay contained to the class actually responsible for that concern, limiting the scope of potential side effects.

questionText: Which statement is true about testing SRP-compliant vs. SRP-violating classes?
option1: Only interfaces can be unit tested, never classes
option2: SRP-violating classes are always easier to test
option3: Testing difficulty is unrelated to SRP
option4: SRP-compliant classes are generally easier to unit test in isolation since they have fewer, more focused dependencies
correctOptionExplanation: A class with one responsibility typically has fewer entangled dependencies, making it simpler to set up and test in isolation.

questionText: Can SRP be applied beyond individual classes, e.g., to modules or microservices?
option1: Yes, but only within a single file
option2: No, SRP is strictly limited to individual classes only
option3: Yes, the 'single reason to change' idea scales to functions, classes, modules, and even service boundaries
option4: No, SRP only applies to interfaces
correctOptionExplanation: The underlying idea, isolating distinct reasons to change, applies at many levels of granularity, including modules and services in a larger system.

questionText: What long-term risk does a codebase face if SRP is consistently ignored?
option1: Fewer classes need to be written overall, which is always good
option2: The codebase automatically becomes faster to run
option3: Classes accumulate unrelated responsibilities over time, becoming large, fragile, and increasingly risky to modify
option4: Unit tests become unnecessary
correctOptionExplanation: Ignoring SRP over time tends to produce sprawling God classes that are hard to understand, test, and safely change — a major long-term maintainability risk.

questionText: Which best explains why SRP reduces the need for extensive regression testing after a change?
option1: Regression testing needs are unrelated to SRP
option2: Because SRP eliminates the need for testing altogether
option3: Because SRP automatically writes regression tests for you
option4: Because a focused class's change only affects its own well-defined responsibility, other parts of the system relying on unrelated responsibilities remain unaffected
correctOptionExplanation: Isolating responsibilities means a targeted change is less likely to have unintended ripple effects elsewhere, reducing how much unrelated functionality needs re-verification.

questionText: From the course notes, decoupling was described using two connected circles labeled 'code 1' and 'code 2' that were tightly coupled. What does breaking that tight coupling typically require?
option1: Making both pieces of code static
option2: Separating unrelated responsibilities into distinct classes/modules so each can change independently
option3: Deleting one of the two pieces of code entirely
option4: Merging code 1 and code 2 into a single larger class
correctOptionExplanation: Decoupling tightly bound code usually means extracting distinct responsibilities into separate units, which is exactly what SRP encourages.

questionText: If a single class's method count keeps growing every sprint to handle new unrelated features, what SOLID principle is most directly being violated?
option1: Liskov Substitution Principle only
option2: Single Responsibility Principle
option3: None, this is expected and healthy growth
option4: Dependency Injection exclusively
correctOptionExplanation: A class continually absorbing new unrelated features is the classic pattern of SRP violation, evolving toward a God class.

questionText: How does SRP support safer parallel feature development across a team?
option1: It prevents more than one feature from being developed per month
option2: Because responsibilities live in separate classes, two developers can add unrelated features without editing the same file or class
option3: It has no impact on parallel development
option4: It requires all developers to work on the same file simultaneously
correctOptionExplanation: Isolated responsibilities in separate classes mean concurrent feature work is less likely to require simultaneous edits to the same code, easing parallel development.

questionText: What is the primary conceptual test to check if a class follows SRP?
option1: Ask: 'is this class public?'
option2: Ask: 'does this class have more than 3 methods?'
option3: Ask: 'does this class implement an interface?'
option4: Ask: 'does this class have more than one reason/stakeholder that could require it to change?'
correctOptionExplanation: The core SRP test is about distinct reasons/actors for change, not surface metrics like method count or visibility.

questionText: Which best describes the overall real-world benefit of consistently applying SRP across a codebase?
option1: Guaranteed zero bugs in production forever
option2: Elimination of the need for any documentation or comments
option3: Safer, faster changes over time — each class has an isolated, well-understood purpose, minimizing regression risk and easing collaboration and testing
option4: Automatic performance improvements in every scenario
correctOptionExplanation: SRP's real payoff is long-term maintainability: isolated responsibilities make the codebase easier to change safely, test, and collaborate on as it grows.

questionText: A Logger class both formats log messages and writes them to multiple destinations (file, console, network). Does this violate SRP?
option1: Only if the Logger class has private fields
option2: Yes, formatting logic and destination/output-writing logic are separate concerns that can each change independently
option3: No, because both relate to 'logging'
option4: No, because Logger is a utility class, and utilities are exempt from SRP
correctOptionExplanation: Message formatting and output-destination handling are independently changeable concerns (e.g., adding a new destination shouldn't require touching formatting logic), so bundling them violates SRP.

questionText: What's the SRP-compliant fix for the Logger example?
option1: Add a giant switch statement inside Logger for every destination
option2: Make Logger a static class with no other changes
option3: Combine Logger with the class that triggered the log event
option4: Separate into a LogFormatter (formats messages) and one or more LogWriter/output classes (handle where messages go)
correctOptionExplanation: Splitting formatting from output-destination handling isolates each responsibility, letting you add new destinations without touching formatting logic and vice versa.
